title: Chaos engineering and game days
subtitle: Break your system on purpose, a little at a time and with a stop button, so you find its weak spots before a real outage does.

c.v: Slack has an internal tool called Confabulator. Engineers use it to change configuration, including during incidents. In one bad incident, it did not work, and the team had to deploy the change by hand.
The tool had an emergency mode. When Slack itself was down, emergency mode skipped the check that needed Slack. On paper, that was the
So the team rebuilt the failure on purpose, in a planned exercise. They cut Confabulator off from Slack and tried a change that did nothing. The error came back.
The cause was small. Both modes posted a notice of each change to a Slack channel. That post had no
. With Slack down, the post hung. The whole request then hit its own time limit before the change was made. So even emergency mode could never finish a change while Slack was down.
Slack then improved its deploy tools and checked the timeout and
A real incident showed the symptom. A planned exercise reproduced it safely and found the cause.
is "the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production."
In plain words: you cause a small, real failure on purpose. Tools call this
. You watch whether users still get what they need. If they do, your confidence grows. If they do not, you found a weak spot while you were ready for it.
is the team version. You plan a failure, everyone who would respond takes part, and you review what happened afterwards.
Every timeout, failover and fallback is a guess until it has run. A chaos experiment runs it on purpose: small, watched, with a stop button, at a time you pick.
Netflix built Chaos Monkey for its move to the AWS cloud. It "randomly disables our production instances", to check that Netflix survives that common failure.
Netflix ran it during business days, "with engineers standing by".
Today the tool still randomly ends virtual machines and containers. Its idea: if engineers see failures often, they build services that survive them.
In April 2011, AWS had a large outage in US-East. Netflix kept running, with more errors and
than usual. But leaving the bad zone took manual work by many teams. Chaos Monkey killed single services, but Netflix did not simulate a whole zone going down.
Engineers started to talk about a "Chaos Gorilla" for that.
By July 2011, Netflix described a whole Simian Army, some of it still only planned. Latency Monkey adds delays between services. Chaos Gorilla would simulate the loss of a whole availability zone.
The site principlesofchaos.org describes an experiment in four steps:
: a measurable output that shows normal behaviour.
Guess that this steady state will continue in a control group and in an experimental group.
Add real-world events, such as servers that crash or network links that are cut.
Try to prove the guess wrong, by looking for a difference between the two groups.
It then gives five advanced principles:
Build a hypothesis around steady state behaviour.
Measure the system's outputs, such as throughput or errors, not its internal attributes.
Pick events by impact or by how often they happen. Include non-failures, like a traffic spike.
Real traffic is "the only way to reliably capture the request path".
Some short-term harm is allowed, but the chaos engineer must keep it small and contained.
An experiment is not a test

A test checks a behaviour you already know, and it passes or fails. An experiment asks a question about the whole system under real conditions. The principles say chaos "verifies that the system does work, rather than trying to validate how it works."
AWS asks you to do both. Keep your normal resilience tests, and add chaos experiments to find what you did not know.
Once an experiment passes, AWS suggests keeping it as an automated regression test in your pipeline.
Step through an example experiment on a checkout service. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
AWS gives an example: a payments system that handles 300 transactions a second, with 99% success and a 500 ms round trip.
AWS's template: "If {specific fault} occurs, the {workload name} workload will {describe mitigating controls} to maintain {business or technical metric impact}."
AWS recommends trying each fault in a non-production environment first. There you also check that your stop conditions fire.

Slack runs every exercise in dev first. Then it decides whether to go on to production. It seriously considers stopping if automatic repair did not work, did not work perfectly or was slow. Most of all, it considers stopping if customers would see more than a short, minor rise in latency.

In AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), a stop condition is a CloudWatch alarm. If it fires, FIS stops the experiment, and you cannot resume it.
Pick the time and the people.
AWS suggests off-peak hours for your first production runs.
Netflix ran Chaos Monkey on business days, with engineers standing by.
Pick a quiet time of day when the team is at work and watching. Slack picks a well-announced time, with the experts in one room or video call.
Tell support and operations teams, and give them a way to report trouble.
Bring the system back to a known-good state. Save dashboards and notes with the time and conditions.

What to inject, and with what
Start with the failures your design claims to survive. AWS lists: lost instances, a database
, CPU and memory stress, added latency, dropped
failures. To test a fallback, block a third-party provider for seconds or hours.
Slack's Confabulator exercise shows that a config tool can be a weak spot too.
Gremlin groups its faults into three kinds. Resource faults use up CPU, memory or disk. State faults shut down hosts, kill
or move the clock ("Time Travel"). Network faults add latency, drop packets or block traffic.

are open-source tools. FIS can run their faults too, for example on a Kubernetes pod.
Any tool should track the experiment's state, log what it does and undo it. AWS discourages home-made scripts that cannot do these.
Gremlin's agent undoes its faults if it loses its connection. But a shutdown or a killed process cannot be rolled back.
A game day tests people and processes, not only machines. AWS says to involve the same teams who would handle a real event. Business decision makers should take part too.
Google's yearly test is called DiRT. It breaks live systems, and it also keeps key people and leaders from helping.
mentioned it; here is what it found. In one test, exactly one person found the emergency phone bridge. In the next drill, more than 100 people found it, but the bridge held only 40 callers.
Give the game day clear roles. Slack has one or two hosts who write a detailed plan, with exact commands and a hypothesis.
Google's DiRT has a technical team, a coordination team and a command center ready to undo a test.
Run the scenario, and then watch. Slack's advice is to hold back and let the system heal itself.

Did any users notice? Did any humans have to step in?

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: If nobody knows, plan an experiment.
Write the hypothesis and the stop condition before the fault. Get one other engineer to review it.
Start with one instance in staging. Then 1% in production, at a quiet time when people are at work and watching.
Turn every finding into a tracked
with an owner, then rerun the experiment.
After a pass, add the experiment to the pipeline so it keeps passing.
"Here is our service's dependency list and the timeouts in our config. For each dependency, suggest one chaos experiment: the fault, the steady-state metric, the hypothesis and a stop condition."
"Write an AWS FIS experiment template that adds 3 seconds of latency to 1% of tasks in the checkout ECS service for 10 minutes. Use the CloudWatch alarm checkout-p99-high as the stop condition."
"Draft a game day plan for losing our primary database: roles, timeline, the exact commands, what we watch, when we abort, and the debrief questions."
Check the selected resources. A wrong tag or filter can hit all instances, not 1%.
Make the alarm fire in staging before you trust it.
Know how to stop the fault by hand, and whether it can be undone at all.
Check every fault name against the tool's docs. An agent can invent ones that do not exist.

q.v: In a chaos experiment, what is the steady state?

options.v: The state of each server's CPU and memory before the test.
A measurable output that shows the system works normally, such as successful orders per second.
The moment when the experiment ends and the system is back to normal.

why.v: The principles say to focus on the system's measurable output, not its internal parts. You compare that output with and without the fault.

q.v: You know your service has no fallback when the cache is down. Should you run a chaos experiment that kills the cache in production?

options.v: Yes, because the experiment will prove the problem to your manager.
No. Fix the known weak spot first. An experiment you know will fail teaches you nothing new.
Yes, but only on a Friday evening, when traffic is low.

why.v: AWS says not to run an experiment when you know the workload will fail. Google lets such services "prefail" and skip the test.

q.v: Your first production experiment adds latency for 1% of users. What should end it automatically if users are hurt?

options.v: A stop condition, an alarm on a steady-state metric that stops the experiment.
The on-call engineer, who checks the dashboard the next morning.
Nothing. Experiments must always run to the end, or the data is useless.

why.v: AWS FIS stops an experiment when a CloudWatch alarm you chose fires. A person can also press stop, but the alarm does not wait for anyone.

q.v: Google's first DiRT test of its emergency phone bridge found that only one person joined. What did the next drill find?

options.v: Everyone joined, and the plan worked.
More than 100 people found the bridge, but it held only 40 callers.
Nobody joined, so the bridge was removed.

why.v: Each drill fixed one problem and showed the next one. That is why you repeat game days.
